headline: Explain the work—not just the AI tool
body:
If you used an approved AI tool on a piece of work, the awkward question is often not whether to mention it—it is how to explain your contribution without making the work sound like one button press.

First, follow any employer, client, professional or legal disclosure rule. Then make your judgement visible: say what the tool did, what you checked and what outcome you remained responsible for. For example: “I used our approved AI tool to compare the first drafts. I checked every recommendation against the source material and rewrote the final advice. That gave the team a faster comparison without outsourcing the decision.”

Atlassian’s 2026 experiment asked 961 U.S. knowledge workers to rate the same hypothetical colleague and business-proposal email. When the note said AI was used, participants rated the colleague more harshly. Describing the team or client benefit reduced—but did not erase—that penalty. This is one hypothetical-work study, not a universal rule and not permission to hide required use.

The AI parallel: context changes how an evaluator interprets an output. A tool name alone says almost nothing about the work. The goal, evidence and human check show what happened. The comparison stops there: your career, workplace rules and reputation are not a prompt experiment.

Try this today: write your explanation in three lines—AI did; I checked; the team or client gained.
